entry.summary: Tyler, The Creator’s Camp Flog Gnaw returned for its 12th year at LA’s Dodger Stadium, and after watching videos from his headlining set, I remain convinced that he’s one of the greatest living performers. During the set, the musician revealed that he didn’t really feel like performing this year, but those fortunate enough to be…
entry.content:
Tyler, The Creator’s Camp Flog Gnaw returned for its 12th year at LA's Dodger Stadium, and after watching videos from his headlining set, I remain convinced that he’s one of the greatest living performers. During the set, the musician revealed that he didn’t really feel like performing this year, but those fortunate enough to be in attendance were treated to an unforgettable, pilot-themed spectacle.

He made his entrance by landing onstage via plane for a 22-track set, dressed as a pilot and performing atop the wings of a massive prop airplane. He also reached into the vault, dusting off rarities from his Cherry Bomb and Bastard eras. He performed “Seven” for the first time since 2014 and “VCR” for the first time since 2019. “BLOW MY LOAD” and “FIND YOUR WINGS” made their live debuts, while “OKAGA, CA” was performed live for the first time since 2015. He also delivered the live debut of his cover of Quavo’s “Baby Breath.” Meanwhile, the crowd went wild for fan favorite “November,” which he hadn’t performed since 2019.

Check out clips below.

He was not fucking around. They played God Hates Us All cuts “God Send Death,” for the first time since 2016, and “Bloodline,” for the…
entry.content:
Slayer played LA's Kia Forum last night for their Reign In Blood anniversary tour. The performance included a few live rarities and a lecture to the crowd from vocalist Tom Araya. He was not fucking around.

They played God Hates Us All cuts “God Send Death,” for the first time since 2016, and “Bloodline,” for the first time since 2017. They also played “The Antichrist” from Show No Mercy for the first time live since 2017. Araya’s rant came about when they were about to perform “Seasons In The Abyss,” but were delayed due to safety concerns. Araya said that the fire marshal told them to pause until things settled down. 

“I don’t know how many times I’ve had this conversation when we first started playing in huge places. I kept telling everyone, man you got to maintain yourself. You can’t start destroying shit because they’ll shut this shit down,” he said. Then he mocks the crowd who begin to boo in response to his reasonable request.

“Listen if you guys want to have fun, you have to come right here in front of us in the middle area where there’s nothing to destroy — except each other. If you start doing shit on the outside of that line right there, they’re gonna shut the place down. They don’t want anyone to get hurt.” He continues on about being respectful to those around you, particularly people sitting in chairs.

entry.content:
The Red Hot Chili Peppers had a playful homage planned for producer Rick Rubin last night at the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame. Rubin produced eight of RHCP’s albums, so naturally they honored Rubin by preforming "Give It Away" in Rubin-esque wigs and beards. They had to start their performance over due to some technical difficulties, but that didn't keep them from rocking out.

Rubin was inducted by Neil Young, who worked with the producer on his 2022 Crazy Horse World Record and has recorded other projects at his Shangri-La studios. Young gave a very long speech tracing Rubin's career. Then Rubin gave possibly the shortest acceptance speech ever: "You can't kill rock 'n' roll." Beastie Boys' Licensed To Ill, one of Rubin's most famous productions, was released 40 years ago today, and he is also credited with conceiving Aerosmith and Run-DMC's classic "Walk This Way" collaboration the same year, Aerosmith and Run-DMC closed the show with that song.

Last night's performers and presenters were all a surprise and the event did not livestream. It will air on ABC on Dec. 8, then stream on Disney+. Check out some clips below.

entry.title: Phoebe Bridgers Glows On SNL
entry.summary: Last night’s episode of SNL was hosted by comedian John Mulaney, with Phoebe Bridgers as the musical guest. entry.content:
Last night's episode of SNL was hosted by comedian John Mulaney, with Phoebe Bridgers as the musical guest. It marked Mulaney's seventh time hosting, and he returned with many of his usual comedic signatures, including a massive, NYC-inspired musical bit. His monologue took a few jabs at baby boomers and the generational beef between them and Gen Z. He also delivered a lengthy impression of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

The cold open featured a CIA meeting bringing together some of the biggest names in tech — James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, and Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — to "learn the difference between a woman who would actually want to have sex with you and a woman who is clearly a spy." The sketch nodded to the recent scandal involving Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who reportedly stepped down from his position after revelations of an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Former cast member Bowen Yang returned as Huang.

This year's musical bit centered on new legislation banning horse-drawn carriages in Central Park following concerns over animal abuse and civilian deaths. Veronika Slowikowska delivered a stunning vocal performance as a woman who spends weeks finishing the NYC Marathon, while Kenan Thompson sang as the cloud of weed smoke hovering over Manhattan. Bowen Yang also appeared as Mary Todd Lincoln, reprising the character from Cole Escola's hit show Oh, Mary!

Another standout was a Woodstock sketch imagining how the baby boomer generation would do a complete 180 by 1985 — becoming increasingly corporate, buying houses, and pushing amphetamines and other stimulants.

This marked Bridgers' third time performing on SNL, including one appearance with boygenius. She performed "Bobby" and "Still Standing." She kicked off "Bobby" with a hearty scream as smoke covered the floor, giving the set a ~spooky~ atmosphere. Things only got more haunting with "Still Standing." She wore a white lace dress and seemingly understated makeup, but that all changed during the final third of the song, when blacklighting revealed a skeletal face and made her white dress glow. There was no guitar smashing this time, but it was a deeply moving performance. For "Bobby," she was backed by her touring band, which includes Melina Duterte of Jay Som.

SNL also announced its next live show, airing December 5, with first-time host Amanda Seyfried and first-time musical guest Don Toliver. Watch clips from last night's show below.

Travis Barker inducted him and played drums on Cynthia Erivo’s cover of Collins’…
entry.content:
Phil Collins made a rare public appearance last night for his second induction into the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame. He’s already been recognized for his work with ‘60s rock group Genesis, but last night he was honored for his solo work. Travis Barker inducted him and played drums on Cynthia Erivo's cover of Collins' iconic 1981 debut solo single "In The Air Tonight."

Collins suffers from a spinal injury and nerve damage resulting from decades of intense drumming. During Genesis' 2021-2022 reunion/farewell tour, he sang sitting down while his song Nick played the drums. However, Collins hinted in interviews leading up to last night's ceremony that returning to the stage is not out of the question, and that he does have song ideas. The last original song Collins released was "Look Through My Eyes" from the soundtrack to Disney's Brother Bear 23 years ago.

Accepting his Rock Hall honor, he said he was doing better these days ("I'm really not as bad as it looks") and that "you haven't heard the last of me, I can promise you that." Three of his Collins' children — Joely, Nic, and Lily — were in attendance. Stereogum spoke to him on the red carpet and asked some normal questions, but here is a clip of some him talking about a Genesis deep cut, his archnemesis Noel Gallagher, and serial killers. ("I know more about serial killers than I do about music now," Collins said in one of multiple interviews that touched on the topic recently.)

This year's performers and presenters were all a surprise and the event did not livestream. It will air on ABC on Dec. 8, then stream on Disney+. But there was an audience in LA's Peacock Theater, so you can watch some videos below.

A couple months ago, Sienna Spiro was listening to Sade while getting ready for fashion week, and last night she sang one of the legendary band's songs at the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame. Spiro took the stage to sing the iconic, TikTok- beloved 1984 hit "Smooth Operator." Andra Day delivered the induction speech.

The soulful sophisti-pop trailblazers Sade — composed of members Sade Adu, Paul Denman, Stuart Matthewman and Andrew Hale — were not there to witness the performance. Earlier this week the band shared the news that they would not be attending the event, but that they do not take the recognition for granted. It was not a shock. "Sade show up to nothing, man," said Method Man of fellow 2026 inductees Wu-Tang Clan the other day. "You ever seen a Sade interview?"

entry.content:
Mere days after Iron Maiden were announced as part of this year's Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame class, the band revealed they would not attend the induction ceremony. Although frontman Bruce Dickinson has previously called the Rock Hall "an utter and complete load of bollocks," the reason for their absence is less hostile: They're on tour in Australia right now. So as with so many of the other absent inductees, the Rock Hall threw together a tribute performance instead.

In Maiden's honor, a supergroup featuring St. Vincent, Metallica's Kirk Hammett and Robert Trujillo, Mötley Crüe's John 5, and Rage Against The Machine's Brad Wilk covered "The Trooper." Jack Black, who inducted Iron Maiden, joined in too. This year's performers and presenters were all a surprise and the event did not livestream. It will air on ABC on Dec. 8, then stream on Disney+. However, there was an audience in LA's Peacock Theater, so you can watch some video below.

entry.title: Deftones & Lauren Mayberry Cover Joy Division & New Order With Peter Hook At Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame 2026
entry.summary: Joy Division and New Order were collectively inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame last night. Though technically separate bands, the two acts represent a continuum; Joy Division’s surviving members formed New Order after the 1980 death of Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis. Together, the groups were nominated for the Rock Hall in…
entry.content:
Joy Division and New Order were collectively inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame last night. Though technically separate bands, the two acts represent a continuum; Joy Division's surviving members formed New Order after the 1980 death of Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis. Together, the groups were nominated for the Rock Hall in 2023 and 2025 before making it in this year.

Bassist Peter Hook, who left the band in 2007 and later engaged in a lengthy legal battle with his former bandmates over disputed royalties, was the only member of New Order to attend tonight's induction. In the lead-up to the ceremony, he said he wouldn't appear at the podium with the other members of the band — "not after what they did to me and my family" — but might be willing to perform with them again if they apologized.

But a reunion performance was not in the cards, as none of the rest of New Order showed. After announcing their departure from New Order in June, drummer Stephen Morris and keyboardist Gillian Gilbert, a married couple, announced that they wouldn't the attend the Rock Hall induction due to Gilbert's cancer battle. Singer-guitarist Bernard Sumner also wasn't present. Hook did not mention his former bandmates in his speech and, in the press room afterwards, he reiterated there would never be a reunion because of what they did to him and his family. (Speaking of which, Hook's son Jack Bates came straight to the ceremony from performing with the Smashing Pumpkins at Darker Waves Festival in Huntington Beach; he's their touring bassist.)

In New Order's stead, Hook was joined by Deftones and Chvrches' Lauren Mayberry to play a pair of classics. Hook and company did Joy Division's iconic "Love Will Tear Us Apart" with Deftones' Chino Moreno on lead vocals. Then Mayberry took the lead for New Order's also-iconic "Bizarre Love Triangle."

Joy Division and New Order were inducted last night by Trent Reznor who covered Joy Division's "Dead Souls" on The Crow soundtrack in '94. Reznor, Deftones, and Mayberry's appearances were not announced in advance. This year's performers and presenters were all a surprise and the event did not livestream. It will air on ABC on Dec. 8, then stream on Disney+. However, there was an audience in LA's Peacock Theater, so you can watch some video below.

entry.content:
More information about the GTA VI soundtrack has leaked. So far, only a select few songs from the 34-track LP have been announced, including “Flower In A Hurricane,” the Justice x Tame Impala x SZA x King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard collaboration that recently earned King Gizz their first-ever Hot 100 entry. Now, however, a newly leaked image of the album’s vinyl tracklist — which Rolling Stone confirms is legit — has revealed additional artists, including Lana Del Rey, Dua Lipa, Arca, Fcukers, Zara Larsson, and Justice featuring the recently in-the-news Michael McDonald, among others.

Del Rey has further involvement with GTA VI: A month ago it was revealed that she would co-host one of the game's in-game radio stations with her husband and Morgan Wallen.

Other artists reportedly featured on the tracklist include Omar Apollo, Kali Uchis & Helado Negro, Rose Gray, Don Toliver, Tee Grizzley, Gunna, Burna Boy, Young Thug, Kodak Black, Camila Cabello, Cardi B, Rina Sawayama, and Playboi Carti. Earlier this week, Tove Lo shared her contribution "Blood In Your Eyes."

The game drops Thursday, with the full soundtrack set to arrive the following day. On Saturday Nov. 21, a Miami festival featuring artists from the soundtrack, including Cardi B, Kodak Black, and Don Toliver, is also scheduled to take place. On Dec. 11, a 50-song original score by Justice will be released — a separate release from the soundtrack album.

entry.title: The 5 Best Songs Of The Week
entry.summary: Every week the Stereogum staff chooses the five best new songs of the week. The eligibility period begins and ends Thursdays right before midnight. You can hear this week’s picks below and on Stereogum’s Favorite New Music Spotify playlist, which is updated weekly. (An expanded playlist of our new music picks is available to subscribers on Spotify and Apple…
entry.content:
Every week the Stereogum staff chooses the five best new songs of the week. The eligibility period begins and ends Thursdays right before midnight. You can hear this week’s picks below and on Stereogum’s Favorite New Music Spotify playlist, which is updated weekly. (An expanded playlist of our new music picks is available to subscribers on Spotify and Apple Music, updated throughout the week.)

5

Kristin Hersh - "Pass Christian"

"This is sunshine in a jar." That's what Kristin Hersh's words say, anyway. Her voice says something else. For decades, Hersh has been one of left-of-center rock music's great spirit summoners, an otherworldly warbler with a cutting wit and a taste for the expansive. On a track that might as well be a throwaway — the lead single from the vinyl-only post-album EP — Hersh takes us on one of her heaviest trips yet. Per the credits, Hersh played every instrument on "Pass Christian," and she made her fuzz-drenched space-rock leads drip with as much dread as her voice. It's like she suddenly decided to make her own Earth-style drone-blues-metal and succeeded wildly. When she harmonizes with herself on the chorus, the beauty makes through, so maybe it really is sunshine in a jar. —Tom

4

Palehound - "Natural Disasters"

"Natural Disasters" is one of those songs that puts everything in perspective. Things are really bad — can’t we all just get through it together? El Kempner puts it in much more poignant terms: "There is no time to left to judge when/ Natural disasters are closing in on us/ And you’re still holding a fucking grudge.” The music is understated, built around a woven melody of guitar plucks and soft piano embellishments. It grows subtly, with shuffling drums, claps, and the occasional bell ring. Kempner sings of happiness at a distance, of finding peace in boundaries. It’s not a flashy ode that hammers home its sentiment, but rather one delivered with a compassionate, somewhat pragmatic sensibility. Even in its seeming simplicity, the song showcases the power of Kempner’s writing.

“Natural Disasters” isn’t a holiday song. But as the end of the year approaches and winter brings on its familiar self-reflection, just as we all reach peak exhaustion, the song feels timely. I’d hate to end this blurb with some yada yada about forgiveness and grace being bigger than any manmade weapons, vices, or treacheries. But if the world’s going to hell anyway, wouldn’t it be nicer to go peacefully than begrudgingly? —Margaret

3

Deloyd Elze - "Yamaha 250"

Deloyd Elze likes to mix up genres, bringing subtle electronics into tender alt-country. Might as well mix up spiritual traditions too, bragging to his lover about arranging a tarot reading right after introducing the refrain, "You set the table/ And I'll say grace." Allen's new song "Yamaha 250" is rich with that kind of lyrical playfulness, and maybe even richer on a musical level. As layers of skittering electronics and rustic strings pile up into gorgeous swells of emotion, so do memorable lines and character flourishes. It's a slice-of-life song that doubles as the sound of a promising musical artist making the leap. —Chris

2

Quiet Light - "Forever"

Quiet Light’s Blue Angel Sparkling Silver 2 made a splash this year because its 12 tracks feel like a soft, bright glimpse into the future of music. But Riya Mahesh’s new tune, “Forever,” is an odyssey back to the ’80s. It’s a sprawling synth-pop love song adorned with dreamy saxophone and a simple but evocative refrain: "All I wanna do is be good to you." More than anything, Quiet Light knows how to transform an emotion into a song, and "Forever" is pure love. —Danielle

1

Armand Hammer - "Assembly Lines"

On this week's surprise-dropped Snakes & Ladders, Armand Hammer haven't lost a step. E L U C I D and billy woods remain masters of abstract sounds and dystopian visions, not least of all on "Assembly Lines." Over Preservation's eerie synth soundscape, the rappers interrogate the intersection of labor and technology in the AI era, coming away with chilling conclusions about workers' fate: "My country, 'tis of thee/ Slavecatcher androids hunt you in electric sheep." —Chris

The band finally broke up in 2022 without explanation, and it was pretty easy to speculate that frontman Dicky Barrett’s anti-vaccine…
entry.content:
Ska-punk hitmakers the Mighty Mighty Bosstones started way back in the early '80s and hit a serious career peak in the late '90s. They kept it going for a long time after that, too. The band finally broke up in 2022 without explanation, and it was pretty easy to speculate that frontman Dicky Barrett's anti-vaccine campaigning had something to do with their decision to call it quits.

Barrett co-wrote a song with Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. to promote one of Kennedy's anti-vaxxer rallies in DC and became a very visible all-around vaccine denier. That position cost Barrett his longtime job as the announcer and Jimmy Kimmel Live!, and he went on to start a band called the Defiant with a bunch of other guys who'd been kicked out of prominent punk bands, seemingly for being anti-vaxxers. But apparently, the Bosstones have figured things out, or at least agreed that their offers are generous enough to let the anti-vaxxer stuff slide.

About a year ago, Barrett joined the Boston hardcore band Haywire for a Bosstones cover, and he's been talking lately about trying to get the band back together. Next spring, British second-wave ska greats Madness will play the Hollywood Bowl. The openers include the Bosstones, along with fellow '90s ska-punk bands Dance Hall Crashers, Goldfinger, and Reel Big Fish. It's going down May 8. If you still haven't caught COVID yet, maybe you can go to that show and pick it up pick it up pick it up.

entry.content:
Back in May, the Detroit rap cult hero Veeze got sick of hearing people ask when he'll drop the follow-up to his much-loved 2023 album Ganger, and he surprise-released an 11-song data-dump mixtape called Y'all Won. That was pretty fun — a new music release, presented as a passive-aggressive get-off-my-back gesture. Now, Veeze has a new proper single, and this one feels a little less like someone had to pry it out of him.

Veeze's new song "guillermoandrade" is as casual as the rest of his music, and its spacey, almost vaporwave beat nicely aligns with his groggy mutter. Supposedly, it's inspired by the designer Guillermo Andradeis. It's about two minutes long, and it suddenly cuts off mid-line, but it's apparently being treated as a single and not a snippet. Mysterious! Check it out.

Just last week, Veeze also appeared on fellow detroit rapper Babyface Ray's single "Nigel Sylvester." The new Babyface Ray album Unfuckwithable 2 is out today, and I feel compelled to tell you that it has a Babyface Ray/Babyface collaboration. Amazing things happening. Here's the "Nigel Sylvester" video.

Unfuckwithable 2 is out now on Wavy Gang/EMPIRE. "guillermoandrade" is out now on Navy Wavy/Warner.

entry.content:
Last year, Scottish rock group Brògeal released a very solid debut album, Tuesday Paper Club, and we dubbed them one of the Best New Artists of 2025. Today, they've returned with a new single for the holidays. It's called "The Last Noel" and features fellow Scottish singer-songwriter Rianne Downey. There are jingle bells! There's accordion! There's melancholy! It feels like a modern classic, with potent storytelling about past lovers.

In a press release, the band shared:

"The Last Noel" is a new offering as a Classic Scottish Christmas song. The tale is told between a man and a woman who haven’t seen each other in quite some time, it is unbeknownst to the couple whether the other is still in love or even still breathing. Every year when the nights turn cold and the Christmas decorations are put up around town and appear down from the loft, the memories of love from previous years come flying back. It also brings back a bitter twinge of the end times of a relationship, and memories are cast back to 'The Last Noel.' The song is a classic tale of love, loss and nostalgia set at Christmas time.

entry.content:
Winston Hightower, the Columbus lo-fi mainstay and Soul Glo member, earned Album Of The Week honors with this year's 100 Acre Wood. That record's guitar-based lo-fi indie-pop made it a perfect match for K Records. But Hightower contains multitudes, and his new project veers in a completely different direction.

Hightower has two new tracks out today under the name Hi-NRG! Both songs, "Handsome Daughter" and "Free Roof, On The House," are electronic pop excursions built on hyperactive rhythms. There's some woozy, pitched-up rapping on the latter song too, which pushes it over the top for me. Imagine an IDM Quasimoto, maybe?

It's always fun to hear an artist known for one kind of music throw themselves into another, and it's especially fun here. Check out both tracks below.

entry.title: 54 Ultra Shares Clairo Collab “Honeymoon”
entry.summary: Listen to Latin soul-inflected indie pop musician 54 Ultra's new single "Honeymoon," written and co-produced by Clairo.
entry.content:
JohnAnthony Rodriguez, the New Jersey singer/songwriter/producer who makes smooth, synthy, Latin soul-inflected indie-pop under the moniker 54 Ultra, has been picking up some buzz since his debut EP First Works dropped in 2025. His latest single, "Honeymoon," clearly has some industry firepower behind it, as Claire Cottrill — Clairo herself! — wrote it and produced it alongside Paul Cherry, Eddie Burns, and William Corduroy.

"Inspired by the sound of late '70s smoky pop music, 'Honeymoon' came together during a magical night at Electric Lady Studios in New York City," Rodriguez says. "I wanted to capture that feeling by recording straight to analog tape and using mostly vintage instruments and equipment, paying close attention to every detail along the way."

"I feel this song is a beautiful step in a new direction for me while still being familiar," he adds. "I even bought a Yamaha CP70 for this song to make sure I got the sound exactly where I wanted it to be. To me, it’s a perfect backdrop to the changing seasons into the end of the year." Listen below.

entry.content:
In 2024, the Brooklyn shoegaze band Crate released exactly one song, "Julia," and we called it perfect. In 2025, they only released one more, "Necklace," and we liked that one too. This year, new Crate music started trickling out, and now the floodgates are open: The band's self-titled debut LP is out today.

Produced by the band's Cody Hudgins and Gift's TJ Freda, Crate weaves the textures of classic shoegaze and slowcore into songs that shimmer and roar, languish and take flight. Songwriters Hudgins and Ezra Engler ensure there's substance beneath the gorgeous veneer, though the sheer beauty of the sound itself is enough to elicit an emotional response

It's an album worth celebrating, and we'll do just that next month in Brooklyn. Stereogum is presenting Crate's album release show Dec. 4 at ErF Studios with support from Whisper Doll, Club Ecology, and Nettle. Get tickets here, and stream the album below.

Crate is out now on Good English. Buy it here.

entry.content:
Brynne Mershon and Naomi Sullins are back with another wonderful Dovetail song. The Hudson Valley dream-pop/indie-folk duo shared "roadkill baby" a couple months ago, and now they're releasing a vivid, lovesick ballad called "sunday night."

"'sunday night' is about accepting what's been lost while still being tethered to it, and the pain of going back to something that does not feel entirely finished," the pair says about the track, which was written in spring of 2024. "The song's composition landed in a transitory period and holds within it transitory themes; the repeating refrain and droning chords seek to create an almost transcendent state, while still remaining grounded in earthy acoustic guitars, with touches of banjo."

Dovetail have always been skilled at conjuring immersive, emotional atmospheres, but the lyrics on "sunday night" are some of their best yet as they delve into storytelling: "That night I went to a party just for the background noise/ The stars told me that I'm alright as I tried to remember your voice." It's lonely, cosmic, and beautiful. Dive in below.

entry.title: Robyn Says Eurovision Is “Just Shit” Now: “It Really Is Embarrassing”
entry.summary: The entire history of Swedish pop music is all tied up with that of the Eurovision Song Contest. entry.content:
The entire history of Swedish pop music is all tied up with that of the Eurovision Song Contest. You could argue that the whole big-bang for Sweden's pop dominance was in 1974, when ABBA's "Waterloo" won Eurovision and rocketed the group to global stardom. But the current version of Eurovision holds absolutely no appeal for Swedish pop queen Robyn. Indeed, Robyn seems to really enjoy talking about how Eurovision sucks now.

In 2023, the Swedish artist Loreen won Eurovision, which meant that Sweden hosted the contest in 2024. When that happened, Robyn was one of more than 1,000 Swedish artists who signed an open letter demanding Israel's exclusion for Eurovision during its ongoing genocide of Palestinian people. But Eurovision has continued to include Israel, even as multiple countries boycott the competition in protest. As it turns out, though, Robyn's objection to Eurovision isn't strictly a genocide-related issue. She just doesn't like it.

Robyn is an elite podcast guest, which you already know if you heard her talking about hating Elon Musk on Las Culturistas earlier this year. Earlier this week, Robyn was on Amy Poehler's Good Hang podcast. Near the end of their interview, Poehler asked Robyn why Eurovision is such a big deal to Europeans, and Robyn immediately busted up laughing. She went on to sketch out Sweden's history of Eurovision greatness and to say that it's "just shit" now. She really put some mustard on the word "shit," too. Here's the full quote.

We don't have ABBA anymore, so I don't really watch Eurovision. They were one of the first people to win the whole thing for us, with "Waterloo." Hard to beat. Then we had [1991 winner] Carola; both me and Zara [Larsson] grew up listening to her. Amazing artist. Now, it's just shit, I would say.

I have American friends that I watch it with. My friend Bart has a blanket that he pulls up over his eyes while we're watching 'cause it's so embarrassing, and it really is embarrassing. And after I watched it, I feel really just overstimulated, and in a bad way. I was looking for words I'm not gonna say. But yeah, I don't like it.

It's a lot more charming to watch her say all that.

Check out the full episode below.

Robyn's very good album Sexistential is out now on Konichiwa/Young.

entry.content:
Last year, Austra unveiled her compelling fifth album Chin Up Buttercup. We were especially fans of the brash lead single "Math Equation." Now, the Canadian artist is back with "Bittersweet" and "Chains And Anchors."

"'Bittersweet' was one of my favorites from the Buttercup era but didn't quite fit on the LP," Katie Stelmanis explains. "I'm glad it's having its moment now. And 'Chains And Anchors' is a track I wrote with Sean Nicholas Savage, a crooner pop songwriting master (in addition to 'Look Me In The Eye' from the LP), with a totally reimagined weirdo production from my collaborator Kieran Adams."

Earlier this year, Austra released a short film called Chin Up Buttercup: The Movie and announced Canadian tour dates. Check them out below along with the new songs.
